source.title: RL on Incorrect Synthetic Data Scales the Efficiency of LLM Math Reasoning by Eight-Fold
source.authors: Amrith Rajagopal Setlur; Saurabh Garg; Xin-Yang Geng; Naman Garg; Virginia Smith; Aviral Kumar

record.tranche_reason: Tests data-scaling and downstream math performance in synthetic-data fine-tuning, using a different measure and training setup from pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper measures held-out GSM8K and MATH performance as synthetic fine-tuning data is scaled, and reports fitted error exponents and non-monotonic cases. It does not measure pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute, nor test compute-optimal allocations. Cited results from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits a power law (Zhang et al. form) to downstream test error as synthetic fine-tuning data grows on GSM8K and MATH. It also reports data-scaling curves that flatten or worsen. This is a fine-tuning regime, so it bears only on V5. It does not vary parameters, pretraining tokens or compute, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add that the authors find positive synthetic data from capable models scales underwhelmingly (error about D^-0.05 to D^-0.15, much slower than pretraining). Scaling self-generated positives can plateau or reverse because of spurious steps. Per-step negatives restore consistent gains equivalent to 8× more data.
record.recipe_differences: The paper scales synthetic fine-tuning data and evaluates downstream math benchmark error or accuracy, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling outcomes depend on the training method and data construction: positive SFT, self-generated RFT, standard DPO, and per-step DPO produce different trends; fixed-question RFT can plateau or worsen. Results are reported separately for GSM8K and MATH.

fits_no_version.finding: RFT on self-generated positives matches SFT trained on 2× the synthetic data, and per-step DPO matches 8× the data (effective data multipliers).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The training method on fine-tuning data shifts the data-scaling curve by a constant effective-data multiplier.

record.problems: The reported scaling-law exponents and several trend comparisons are not accompanied by uncertainty estimates in the text. Some plotted values are not stated numerically. The exponents' associated model is not specified in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The star-graph didactic analysis (Section 6.3.4 and Figure 11) varies training iterations and examines generalization on a synthetic graph task, not the scaling quantities or downstream math benchmarks covered by these versions. Qualitative examples of identified spurious steps are also omitted because they do not report a separate scaling result.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small to large runs.
Model shape at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated-data pretraining, transfer; also how well the power law fits (no goodness-of-fit is reported).
Downstream performance vs model scale or pretraining loss; only fine-tuning data size is varied.
Effects of parameter counting, schedule or fitting method on exponents; compute-optimal splits.

missing.what: Llama2-7B SFT data-scaling curves on GSM8K and MATH (plotted alongside DeepSeek)
Pass@5 error also follows similar power-law trends with data size
Authors' statement that fine-tuning data exponents are much weaker than pretraining scaling

record.verdict_notes: Downstream error is varied only against fine-tuning data size, at fixed 7B models, so this is a fine-tuning-regime test of V5, not V6. Most rows are method comparisons and are unlinked. No uncertainty or fit quality is reported for the exponents.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether small-run pretraining-loss fits predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and how either grows with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated-data pretraining, transfer, and whether the original pretraining-loss law carries over to those settings.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or model scale.
Parameter-counting choices, training schedules as a source of exponent differences, and compute-optimal allocation fits.
